Eggs of the Spotted sandpiper (Actitis macularius) are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] in the female-dominated care system characteristic of this species, and development proceeds over a period typically lasting between 20 and 24 days (20-24 days) [ab = 20-24 days] at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The newly hatched chick emerges at a wet weight of 6.05 grams [Wwb = 6.05 grams], a modest mass that reflects the substantial yolk investment allocated to the calcareous egg. This neonatal mass is notably lower than the initial wet weight of 9 grams [Ww0 = 9 grams] that has been recorded for the yolked ovum itself, underscoring the energetic cost of embryogenesis and the metabolic demands of tissue differentiation sustained throughout the incubation period. The relatively short incubation duration at this thermal regime is consistent with the semi-precocial developmental mode of this species, in which downy chicks are capable of leaving the nest within hours of hatching despite still relying on parental brooding for thermoregulation. Field records indicate that incubation temperatures may fluctuate slightly around this baseline, but the 22-day mean (22 days) [ab = 22 days] represents a reliable benchmark under stable nesting conditions when incubation is carried out at 36 °C [T = 36 °C].

Under the active metabolic conditions typical of the species when maintained at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the fledgling stage is reached at 20 days after hatching [tx = 20 days after hatching], a developmental milestone that marks the achievement of sustained flight and the transition away from complete nest dependence. This rapid feather maturation is characteristic of the sandpiper's life history, allowing juveniles to escape ground predators and exploit intertidal foraging zones earlier than many similarly sized shorebirds. This interval between fledging and reproductive activation reflects the continued growth of skeletal and muscular systems necessary for the energetically demanding courtship displays and territorial defense that define the breeding system of this species. The 41 °C [T = 41 °C] threshold represents the body temperature range during active foraging and display periods.

The first successful breeding event typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] when birds are maintained at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], a delay that reflects the extended period required for territory acquisition and pair bond formation in this polyandrous species. Unlike many other small Charadriiformes that breed in their first spring, the Spotted sandpiper defers reproduction until the second calendar year, a life-history strategy that likely enhances reproductive output by allowing individuals to accumulate sufficient fat reserves for the high energetic demands of multiple clutches. The ultimate wet weight of adult females reaches 48 grams [Wwi = 48 grams], while males are appreciably smaller, attaining an ultimate wet weight of 36.9 grams [Wwi = 36.9 grams]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism is reversed relative to the typical avian pattern and aligns with the female-dominated territorial system in which larger body size confers advantages in competition for access to multiple mates. Adult body mass is a strong predictor of reproductive success in this species.

The maximum longevity of the Spotted sandpiper under field conditions has been documented at 12 years [am = 12 years] when measured at the typical active body temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], a lifespan that distinguishes it from many smaller sandpipers with shorter adult survival. This extended lifespan is consistent with a life-history strategy in which reproductive effort is distributed across multiple seasons rather than concentrated into a single explosive breeding episode. A female can lay between 1 and 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 4 eggs per clutch], and field observations indicate that she typically completes 1.7 clutches per year [F_R_i = 1.7 clutches per year], a reproductive frequency that translates to a substantial annual output for a bird of this body size. The combination of moderate clutch size and high clutch frequency is unusual among scolopacid sandpipers and may reflect the female's ability to offload incubation duties onto multiple males, thereby freeing time for additional nesting attempts within a single season. This polyandrous breeding system drives the species' high reproductive potential.

Comparative analyses of body mass trajectories in Spotted sandpipers reveal that juveniles undergo a period of rapid mass increase during the first weeks post-hatching, with the 6.05 gram [Wwb = 6.05 gram] birth mass more than doubling within the first ten days of exogenous feeding. The initial 9 gram [Ww0 = 9 gram] wet weight of the fertilised ovum illustrates the considerable maternal investment per egg, particularly given that a female's own body mass at the start of the breeding season is only 48 grams [Wwi = 48 grams]. The 36.9 gram [Wwi = 36.9 gram] asymptotic mass of males indicates that the sexual size dimorphism emerges early in development and is maintained throughout adulthood. The maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] at 41 °C [T = 41 °C] provides a temporal framework for understanding the species' slow pace of reproduction relative to other members of the genus Actitis, which typically show shorter life expectancies. Lifetime reproductive output is therefore mediated more by the number of breeding seasons than by annual fecundity per se.
